variants.name: Swing passive view with ActionListener forwarding
variants.idiom_name: interface implemented by a JPanel + ActionListener/lambda forwarding to the presenter
variants.implementation_notes: The classic Java realization: an interface (or abstract class) declares the view's semantic operations, the JPanel/JFrame implements it, and each widget's listener forwards the gesture to a presenter method - typically an ActionListener lambda calling presenter.queryChanged(). The presenter holds the interface and the model and contains no Swing types, so plain JUnit runs it with a stub view. Prefer this form with Swing/AWT or SWT; the classic structure is exactly what the JDK's listener model expects.
pitfalls: Swing is single-threaded: presenter results arriving on a worker thread must be published with SwingUtilities.invokeLater, or the component tree corrupts silently.
Listeners registered on shared models keep the panel reachable; remove them (or use weak listeners) when the screen is disposed or reused.
Anonymous inner classes and lambdas are convenient but make removal hard - keep a named reference if the subscription must be detachable.

variants.name: JavaFX FXML controller with property binding
variants.implementation_notes: In JavaFX the FXML loader builds the scene graph and injects the controls into a controller, so the view is already a passive declaration and the controller can act as the presenter: bindings (label.textProperty().bind(...), StringProperty/BooleanProperty, ChangeListener) replace manual field updates, and complex effects go through listeners. This is the Supervising Controller shape - simple mapping is declarative, the controller handles input and the hard cases. Use it where the screen is defined in FXML; keep the plain interface form when the presenter must also be testable without the JavaFX toolkit (bindings need the FX thread and toolkit classes).
pitfalls: JavaFX bindings must be created and updated on the FX application thread; a background computation has to hop back with Platform.runLater.
Bindings use weak listeners (the bound property can be collected), so a property held only by a binding may disappear silently - keep strong references to the source properties.
Binding and manual set on the same property throws at runtime (a bound property cannot be set); choose one direction per property.
